name: ישר ומישור במרחב
questiontext:
Different lines and planes in \(R^3\) admit a variety of mutual configurations. We can find all possibilities in this little figure as follows:

    

For a line and a plane there are three possibilities:

(1) The line \(n\) is parallel to the plane \(X\), (2) The line \(m\) intersects both planes \(X,Y\), (3) The line \(n\) is contained in the plane \(Y\). 

For a two planes there are again three possibilities:

(1) The planes \(X\) and \(Y\) are parallel, (2) The planes \(X\) and \(Z\) intersect in a line, (3) The plane \(X\) coincides with itself. 

Consider the plane \(P: \left\{v \in R^3 \ | \ v \cdot {{CT:0}} = {{CT:1}} \right\} \) and the line \(\ell: {{CT:2}} + Span \left( {{CT:3}} \right) \)

Find a vector \(0 \ne n \in R^3\) normal to the plane \(P\). Namely a vector \(n\) such that \(n \cdot (w_1 - w_2) = 0, \  \forall w_1,w_2 \in P \). Make sure that you understand why this is the what is required of a normal (=orthogonal) vector to the plane!

\(n\)  = [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] 

How to enter: each entry in its own box: a number, a fraction (e.g. 1/2) or an expression (e.g. sqrt(2)).

What is the cosine of the angle between the direction of the line and the normal to the plane

\(cos(\angle(n, v)) = \) [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]]

What is their mutual configuration (enter a number 1=parallel, 2=intersecting, 3=the line is contained in the plane):

[[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]]

What is the distance between \(P\) and \(\ell\) [[input:ans4]] [[validation:ans4]].

prts.feedbackvariables: ngood: if (ans1 = zervect) then false else (if (crossprod(n,ans1)=zervect) then true else false);

on_true.feedback: Yes the vector {@ans1@} is clearly normal (=orthogonal) to the plane \(P\) just by the equation defining this plane:  \(v \cdot {{CT:0}} = {{CT:1}}\). Of course any nonzero scalar multiple of this vector is also good.
The zero vector is clearly orthogonal to any plane. But you were asked for a non-zero vector.

on_false.feedback: You chose a wrong normal (=orthogonal) vector. An obvious choice would have been the vector {{CT:4}} which is clearly normal to the plane \(P\) just by the equation defining this plane:  \(v \cdot {{CT:0}} = {{CT:1}}\). Of course any nonzero scalar multiple of this vector would also work.

on_true.feedback: You found the correct cosine of the angle between the line and the normal vector.
You found the correct cosine of the angle between the line and the normal vector.

This is the cosine of the angle between the direction of the line and the plane itself. You were asked to find the angle between the same direction and the normal vector \({{CT:0}}\) found in the previous question.

on_false.feedback:
Sorry you got this angle wrong. You are were asked to find the angle between the two vectors \(v={{CT:3}}\) and \(n={{CT:0}}\). This is readily given by the inner product as follows:

\[cos(\angle(v,n)) = \frac{v \cdot n}{||v|| ||n||} = \frac{{{CT:3}} \cdot {{CT:0}}}{\left|\left|{{CT:3}}\right|\right| \left|\left|{{CT:0}}\right|\right|}  = {{CT:5}}.\]

on_true.feedback: Yes, you found the correct mutual configuration of \(P\) and \(\ell\).

on_false.feedback: No, you did not find the correct mutual configuration of \(P\) and \(\ell\).

on_true.feedback: Since \(n\) is not orthogonal to \(v\) we can immediately deduce that the line \(\ell\) intersects the plane \(P\) in one point. One can find this point by solving a system of equations but this is not necessary in order to solve the question.

on_false.feedback:
Since \(n\) is orthogonal to \(v\) we can immediately deduce that the line \(\ell\) is either contained or parallel to the plane \(P.\) In order to distinguish between these two possibilities it is enough to check if \(w \in P\). Of course any other point on the line could serve us just as well. 

In order to determine if \(w \in P\) we just check if it satisfies the equation defining the plane

\[n \cdot w = {{CT:0}} \cdot {{CT:2}} = {{CT:6}}\]

on_true.feedback: Since the equation does not hold we deduce that the line \(\ell\) is parallel to the plane \(P\).

on_false.feedback: Since the equation is satisfied we deduce that the line \(\ell\) is contained in the plane \(P\)

on_true.feedback:
• Since the line and the plane are parallel there is a positive distance between them. In order to find the distance between them let us first find a point on the plane. For example by solving the defining system of equations:

\[{@vec@} \cdot {{CT:0}} = {@vec.n@} = {{CT:1}}\]

One solution of this single equation with three unknowns (x,y,z) has many solutions. One of them for example is \(u = {{CT:7}}\). 

Now we can find the distance by taking a vector \(w-u= {{CT:2}}-{{CT:7}} = {{CT:8}}\) and projecting it on the normal direction. 

\[d = Proj_n(w-u) = \left| \left| \frac{(w-u) \cdot n}{n \cdot n} n \right| \right| = {{CT:9}}\]
Since the plane and the line intersect the distance between them is zero.

on_false.feedback: Since the line is contained in the plane the distance between them is zero.
